extracted.intended_audience: politically engaged British public and legislators (late 18th-century readers)
extracted.subtask_short: political critique of the French Revolution
extracted.subtask_description: A rhetorical-political essay arguing standards for legitimate representative government and warning about the dangers in the composition and conduct of revolutionary assemblies (focused on the French National Assembly).

rubrics_metrics.name: Respectable composition of assemblies
rubrics_metrics.description: The body of an assembly should be 'respectably composed, in point of condition in life, of permanent property, of education, and of such habits as enlarge and liberalise the understanding.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke argues that sobriety and moderation in proposals depend on a broadly respectable composition (stable property, education, enlarged habits). If the mass of an assembly lacks these qualities, even talented leaders will conform to the tastes of the ignorant majority and absurd projects will prevail. Examples/anti-patterns: assemblies composed largely of the poor, uneducated, or mercantile jobbers tend to produce rash or rapacious measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leaders must conform proposals to followers' tastes
rubrics_metrics.description: Leaders 'must conform their propositions to the taste, talent, and disposition of those whom they wish to conduct.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Political leaders cannot lead effectively unless they temper proposals to the capacities and prejudices of their followers; if they fail, they either become mere instruments of absurd projects or must rely on exceptional virtue. This explains why a few talented men embedded in a poor assembly still produce poor outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer practical experience over mere theorists
rubrics_metrics.description: An assembly should include persons with practical experience in state affairs rather than only 'men of theory.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke notes that the Third Estate's deputies largely lacked practical state experience. The absence of practical knowledge makes policy-making rash and disconnected from the realities of governance; practical experience is a qualification for responsible legislation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid assemblies dominated by narrow professional classes
rubrics_metrics.description: When 'supreme authority is vested in a body so composed' of inferior professional practitioners (e.g., provincial advocates, petty magistrates, local attorneys), it produces bad consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assemblies dominated by the mechanical, instrumental parts of professions (unlearned lawyers, petty municipal litigious actors, some doctors, stock-jobbers) will pursue private, litigious, or rapacious interests rather than the public good. Anti-pattern: an assembly where lawyers/mechanics/stock dealers preponderate becomes self-interested and destructive of property and order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation must include ability as well as property
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Nothing is a due and adequate representation of a state, that does not represent its ability as well as its property.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ability (vigorous, active principle) and property (sluggish, inert) must both be represented; because property is vulnerable to invasion by ability, property must be predominant in representation to be protected. Property should be represented in large masses so it forms a defensive rampart against rapacity. Otherwise, property will be destroyed and rational liberty will not exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection of large proprietary interests as stabilizers
rubrics_metrics.description: The power of perpetuating property in families and hereditary distinction (e.g., a house of peers) is a principal security for transmission and the perpetuation of society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke defends institutions (like a hereditary peerage) that secure family wealth and distinction as stabilizing forces. Such proprietors act as ballast for the commonwealth; while they may be flattered or abused, their presence prevents the diffusion and vulnerability of property.

rubrics_metrics.name: No general approval for appointment by lot or rotation
rubrics_metrics.description: 'No rotation, no appointment by lot, no mode of election operating in the spirit of sortition or rotation, can be generally good in a government conversant in extensive objects.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selection methods that ignore duty-fit (lot, rotation) do not tend to select persons fit for complex government. Leaders should be chosen with regard to aptitude for the office; random or purely rotational schemes are inappropriate for high public responsibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Merit should pass through probation
rubrics_metrics.description: Rare merit ought not to be made too easy of access to power; 'it ought to pass through some sort of probation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The road to eminence should include trials and probation; this tests virtue and ensures that those elevated have borne difficulty and struggle. Anti-pattern: facile, immediate elevation from obscure conditions without proof of capacity.

rubrics_metrics.name: No qualification for government except virtue and wisdom
rubrics_metrics.description: 'There is no qualification for government but virtue and wisdom, actual or presumptive.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While Burke argues for the prudence of property and rank in representation, he explicitly permits talent and virtue from any station to hold office; the core criterion for governance is virtue and wisdom, wherever found.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assemblies need constitutional restraints and respected usage
rubrics_metrics.description: An assembly without 'fundamental law, no strict convention, no respected usage to restrain it' is dangerous because it can make a constitution to suit its designs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke warns that once old orders are destroyed and no customary restraints remain, an assembly can claim unlimited power to remake the constitution to its will. Good governance requires laws, conventions, and usages that constrain arbitrary remakings of fundamental institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware arithmetic majoritarianism
rubrics_metrics.description: The claim that 'twenty-four millions ought to prevail over two hundred thousand' is naïve if a state's constitution is treated as mere arithmetic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Majority numbers alone do not guarantee good choices; the will and interest of the many frequently differ, and pure numerical dominance can lead to destructive outcomes. Institutions should mediate popular will rather than allow raw numerical supremacy over stabilizing interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid elevating those with scant worldly knowledge to national reform
rubrics_metrics.description: Sending 'country curates' and men who 'knew nothing of the world beyond the bounds of an obscure village' to undertake the 'new-modelling a state' is ill-advised because they may regard property with envy and be tempted into plunder.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Delegates intended to reframe a nation's constitution should possess sufficient worldly knowledge and prudence; electing the deeply impoverished or provincials ignorant of statecraft risks policies motivated by envy and short-term gain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevent central monopolization by a single city
rubrics_metrics.description: A republic composed of many municipalities cannot long be governed as one body if 'the republic of Paris' monopolizes power, the captivity of the king, and the dominion over the Assembly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke warns against a single urban center (Paris) consolidating authority in a federation of local republics; national cohesion requires a functioning capital and mechanisms preventing a single city's dominance and the consequent resentment of other regions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social order requires reasonable preeminence of some classes
rubrics_metrics.description: In societies of mixed descriptions 'some description must be uppermost' and levellers who attempt to equalize all things 'change and pervert the natural order of things.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke contends that some regulated preeminence (not exclusive appropriation) for birth or established classes is neither unnatural nor unjust and contributes to order. Radical leveling risks destabilizing the structure required for a stable polity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware leaders driven by ambition and lust for glory
rubrics_metrics.description: If talented leaders are 'actuated by sinister ambition and a lust of meretricious glory' they will exploit a feeble assembly, making followers 'the dupe and instrument of their designs.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective selection and oversight of leaders must guard against personal ambition and the use of ignorant followers as instruments for private aggrandizement. Anti-pattern: charismatic leaders leveraging an unqualified mass to pursue lucrative opportunities arising from revolution.
